title: Implement Trie II (Prefix Tree)
statement:
Build a class `Trie` that stores a collection of lowercase strings in which the same string may appear several times.

- `Trie()` starts with an empty collection.
- `insert(word)` adds one copy of `word` to the collection.
- `countWordsEqualTo(word)` returns how many copies of exactly `word` the collection holds.
- `countWordsStartingWith(prefix)` returns how many strings in the collection, counting every copy, begin with `prefix` (a string counts as beginning with itself).
- `erase(word)` removes one copy of `word` from the collection. Every call to `erase` is guaranteed to name a string that currently has at least one copy stored.
constraints: word and prefix contain only lowercase English letters
At most 3 * 10^4 calls are made in total to insert, countWordsEqualTo, countWordsStartingWith and erase
erase is only called with a word that is currently stored
notes:
## Intuition

A plain map from word to number of copies answers `countWordsEqualTo` instantly, but `countWordsStartingWith` would have to scan every stored word. A trie shares common prefixes: every prefix of every stored word is exactly one node. If each node also counts how many stored words pass through it, a prefix query becomes a single walk down the trie, and so does every other operation.

## Approach

1. Each node holds `children` (letter → node), `prefixCount` (how many stored copies pass through it) and `endCount` (how many stored copies end exactly there).
2. `insert` walks the word from `root`, creating missing children, adds 1 to `prefixCount` of every node it enters, and adds 1 to `endCount` of the last node.
3. `find(text)` walks `text` and returns its node, or `null` as soon as a letter has no child.
4. `countWordsEqualTo` returns the found node's `endCount`; `countWordsStartingWith` returns its `prefixCount`; both return 0 when `find` gives `null`.
5. `erase` walks the same path as `insert` and subtracts 1 instead. The word is guaranteed to be stored, so every child exists.

## Example 1, step by step

Inserting `"apple"` twice gives the nodes `a`, `ap`, `app`, `appl`, `apple` a `prefixCount` of 2, and `apple` an `endCount` of 2. `countWordsEqualTo("apple")` reads `endCount = 2`; `countWordsStartingWith("app")` reads `prefixCount = 2`. After one `erase("apple")` both numbers drop to 1, so the next two queries return `1` and `1`. After the second erase, `app` has `prefixCount = 0`, so the last query returns `0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L) per call, where L is the length of the word or prefix: each call walks one path.
- Space: O(total letters inserted) for the nodes, since nodes are never removed.

## Pitfalls

- Count copies, not distinct words: inserting the same word twice must add 2 to every count on its path.
- `prefixCount` belongs to the node you step into, not the one you leave; otherwise the root collects counts and the last letter misses one.
- A node left with zero counts after `erase` still exists; the answers stay right because they read the counts, not whether the node is there.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | the empty-prefix node at the top of the trie |
| `node` | the node reached so far while walking a word |
| `letter` | the current character of the word being walked |
| `children` | map from a letter to the child node |
| `prefixCount` | stored copies whose path passes through this node |
| `endCount` | stored copies that end exactly at this node |

narration.29: A missing prefix starts no words; otherwise every word passing through counts.

narration.36: One fewer stored word passes through this node.
narration.38: And one fewer copy ends at the last node.
